📦 What Auto-Claude Is
Auto-Claude is an autonomous multi-session AI coding framework designed to help you plan, build, and validate software using AI agents. It’s published on GitHub under the AGPL-3.0 open-source license. 
GitHub

According to the repository’s README:

🧠 Autonomous Task Handling: You describe a task, and internal agent processes handle planning, coding, and quality validation for you. 
GitHub

GitHub

GitHub

GitHub

# =========================
# AUTO-CLAUDE WINDOWS FIX
# =========================

Write-Host "=== Auto-Claude Full Environment Fix ===" -ForegroundColor Cyan

# 1. Execution policy (safe, user-only)
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Force

# 2. Verify Python launcher exists
if (-not (Get-Command py -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) {
    Write-Error "Python Launcher (py.exe) not found. Install Python from python.org and RE-RUN this script."
    exit 1
}

# 3. Check Python 3.12 availability
$pyList = py -0 2>$null
if ($pyList -notmatch "3.12") {
    Write-Error "Python 3.12 NOT FOUND.
Install Python 3.12.x (64-bit) from https://www.python.org and re-run this script."
    exit 1
}

Write-Host "Python 3.12 detected ✔" -ForegroundColor Green

# 4. Go to Auto-Claude directory
$repo = "$HOME\Auto-Claude"
if (-not (Test-Path $repo)) {
    Write-Error "Auto-Claude directory not found at $repo"
    exit 1
}
Set-Location $repo

# 5. Remove broken venv if exists
if (Test-Path "venv") {
    Write-Host "Removing old virtual environment..."
    Remove-Item -Recurse -Force venv
}

# 6. Create clean venv with Python 3.12
Write-Host "Creating virtual environment (Python 3.12)..."
py -3.12 -m venv venv

# 7. Activate venv
Write-Host "Activating virtual environment..."
& .\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# 8. Upgrade pip tooling
python -m pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel

# 9. Install backend dependencies
Write-Host "Installing backend dependencies..."
pip install -r apps/backend/requirements.txt

# 10. Install test dependencies (non-fatal)
if (Test-Path "tests\requirements-test.txt") {
    pip install -r tests/requirements-test.txt
}

# 11. Install node deps if needed
if (Test-Path "package.json") {
    Write-Host "Installing Node dependencies..."
    npm install
}

# 12. Run Auto-Claude
Write-Host "`n=== STARTING AUTO-CLAUDE ===" -ForegroundColor Cyan
python run.py

$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"

Write-Host "=== AUTO-CLAUDE WINDOWS HARD FIX ===" -ForegroundColor Cyan

# Allow scripts
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Force

# Allow py launcher to auto-install
$env:PYLAUNCHER_ALLOW_INSTALL = "1"

# Ensure winget exists
if (-not (Get-Command winget -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) {
    Write-Error "winget not found. Update Windows App Installer."
    exit 1
}

# Install Python 3.12 silently if missing
$pyList = py -0 2>$null
if ($pyList -notmatch "3.12") {
    Write-Host "Installing Python 3.12.x (64-bit)..." -ForegroundColor Yellow
    winget install --id Python.Python.3.12 --source winget --silent --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements
    Write-Host "Python installed. Restarting shell is NOT required." -ForegroundColor Green
}

# Verify Python 3.12
$pyList = py -0
if ($pyList -notmatch "3.12") {
    Write-Error "Python 3.12 installation failed."
    exit 1
}

Write-Host "Python 3.12 detected ✔" -ForegroundColor Green

# Move to repo
$repo = "$HOME\Auto-Claude"
if (-not (Test-Path $repo)) {
    Write-Error "Auto-Claude not found at $repo"
    exit 1
}
Set-Location $repo

# Remove old venv
if (Test-Path "venv") {
    Write-Host "Removing old venv..."
    Remove-Item -Recurse -Force venv
}

# Create new venv with Python 3.12
Write-Host "Creating clean venv (Python 3.12)..."
py -3.12 -m venv venv

# Activate venv
Write-Host "Activating venv..."
& "$repo\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1"

# Upgrade tooling
python -m pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel

# Install backend dependencies
Write-Host "Installing backend dependencies..."
pip install -r apps/backend/requirements.txt

# Install test deps (optional)
if (Test-Path "tests\requirements-test.txt") {
    pip install -r tests/requirements-test.txt
}

# Install Node deps if needed
if (Test-Path "package.json") {
    Write-Host "Installing Node dependencies..."
    npm install
}

# Run correct backend entrypoint
Write-Host "`n=== STARTING AUTO-CLAUDE ===" -ForegroundColor Cyan
python apps/backend/main.py

Replit Agent Prompt Maker v2 said:
Here’s a clear comparison between the two CPUs you asked about:

🔥 Overall: AMD Ryzen 7 1700X vs AMD Ryzen 5 1600
Which is generally faster?
✅ Ryzen 7 1700X is faster overall, especially in multi-core performance. It has 8 cores and 16 threads compared to the Ryzen 5 1600’s 6 cores and 12 threads, which gives it a notable advantage in tasks that use many cores (like rendering, video encoding, multitasking, etc.). Benchmarks show the 1700X can be ~20–27% faster in aggregate performance scores than the 1600. 
Technical City

Why?

More cores/threads: 8 Cores / 16 Threads vs 6 Cores / 12 Threads — this helps a lot in multi-threaded workloads. 
Technical City

Higher max boost frequencies: The 1700X typically boosts slightly higher (~3.8 GHz) than the 1600 (~3.6 GHz). 
CPU Compare

Single-Core Performance:
They’re pretty similar for single-thread tasks (important for some games and everyday use). Some benchmark sources show only a small difference. 
CPU Benchmark

Gaming Performance:
In many games, the difference can be small or negligible, because many games depend more on GPU and single-core speed than total cores. Some gameplay tests show equal performance in certain titles. 
HowManyFPS

Power & Efficiency:
The Ryzen 5 1600 uses less power (65 W vs 95 W on the 1700X) and often comes with a cooler included, which can make it easier/cheaper to build with. 
CPU Benchmark

📊 Summary
Feature	Ryzen 7 1700X	Ryzen 5 1600
Cores / Threads	8 / 16	6 / 12
Typical Performance	Higher overall	Good, but lower multi-core
Best Use Cases	Heavy multitasking, content creation	Everyday use, budget builds
Gaming	Similar in many games	Similar in many games
Power	Higher (95W)	Lower (65W)
✅ Recommendation
Choose 1700X if you want better overall performance especially for multi-threaded tasks.

Choose 1600 if you want a more power-efficient, lower-cost build with still solid performance.

bl_info = {
    "name": "Nyghtshade Assistant",
    "blender": (3, 0, 0),
    "category": "AI"
}

import bpy

class NyghtshadePanel(bpy.types.Panel):
    bl_label = "Nyghtshade"
    bl_idname = "NYGHTSHADE_PT_main"
    bl_space_type = 'VIEW_3D'

    def draw(self, context):
        layout = self.layout
        layout.operator("nyghtshade.ask_ai")

class AskAI(bpy.types.Operator):
    bl_idname = "nyghtshade.ask_ai"
    bl_label = "Ask AI"

    def execute(self, context):
        # send scene mesh + prompt
        return {'FINISHED'}

def register():
    bpy.utils.register_class(NyghtshadePanel)
    bpy.utils.register_class(AskAI)

def unregister():
    bpy.utils.unregister_class(NyghtshadePanel)

🗣️ Voice Command Grammar — Expanded (Intent Map)
Here’s a more structured grammar resembling SRGS (simplified):

<grammar version="1.0">
  <rule id="root">
    <one-of>
      <item> place <asset> (around | near | inside) <location> </item>
      <item> generate <script_type> for <purpose> </item>
      <item> find <asset_type> </item>
      <item> translate to <language> </item>
      <item> set theme to <theme> </item>
    </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="asset">
    <one-of> crate crates torch torches tree trees npc enemies </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="location">
    <one-of> castle keep forest path road </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="script_type">

</grammar>

🌐 Unity 6 Plugin (C#)
using UnityEditor;
using UnityEngine;

public class NyghtshadeUnityPlugin : EditorWindow
{
    [MenuItem("Nyghtshade/Assistant")]
    public static void ShowWindow() {
        GetWindow<NyghtshadeUnityPlugin>("Nyghtshade");
    }

class AskAI(bpy.types.Operator):

    bl_label = "Ask AI"

    def execute(self, context):
        # send scene mesh + prompt
        return {'FINISHED'}

def register():
    bpy.utils.register_class(NyghtshadePanel)
    bpy.utils.register_class(AskAI)

def unregister():
    bpy.utils.unregister_class(NyghtshadePanel)

bl_info = {
    "name": "Nyghtshade Assistant",
    "blender": (3, 0, 0),
    "category": "AI"
}

import bpy

class NyghtshadePanel(bpy.types.Panel):
    bl_label = "Nyghtshade"
    bl_idname = "NYGHTSHADE_PT_main"
    bl_space_type = 'VIEW_3D'

    def draw(self, context):
        layout = self.layout
        layout.operator("nyghtshade.ask_ai")

class AskAI(bpy.types.Operator):
    bl_idname = "nyghtshade.ask_ai"
    bl_label = "Ask AI"

    def execute(self, context):
        # send scene mesh + prompt
        return {'FINISHED'}

def register():
    bpy.utils.register_class(NyghtshadePanel)
    bpy.utils.register_class(AskAI)

def unregister():
    bpy.utils.unregister_class(NyghtshadePanel)

🗣️ Voice Command Grammar — Expanded (Intent Map)
Here’s a more structured grammar resembling SRGS (simplified):

<grammar version="1.0">
  <rule id="root">
    <one-of>
      <item> place <asset> (around | near | inside) <location> </item>
      <item> generate <script_type> for <purpose> </item>
      <item> find <asset_type> </item>
      <item> translate to <language> </item>
      <item> set theme to <theme> </item>
    </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="asset">
    <one-of> crate crates torch torches tree trees npc enemies </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="location">
    <one-of> castle keep forest path road </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="script_type">
    <one-of> C# Python blueprint behavior </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="language">
    <one-of> English Spanish Chinese French </one-of>
  </rule>

</grammar>
This gives a production grammar that NLP models can map to command intents.

Key Concepts Explained:

Core Services take natural language + voice → interpret it → dispatch to the right tool.

Scene Analyzer reads a scene’s mesh graph and spits out actionable data (surface normals, bounds, slopes, etc.).

Asset Discovery crawls local and remote repos, labels assets, and catalogs them.

Plugin Bridge lets the assistant “live inside” external tools (Unity, Unreal, Blender, VS Code).

bl_info = {
    "name": "Nyghtshade Assistant",
    "blender": (3, 0, 0),
    "category": "AI"
}

import bpy

class NyghtshadePanel(bpy.types.Panel):
    bl_label = "Nyghtshade"
    bl_idname = "NYGHTSHADE_PT_main"
    bl_space_type = 'VIEW_3D'

    def draw(self, context):
        layout = self.layout
        layout.operator("nyghtshade.ask_ai")

class AskAI(bpy.types.Operator):
    bl_idname = "nyghtshade.ask_ai"
    bl_label = "Ask AI"

    def execute(self, context):
        # send scene mesh + prompt
        return {'FINISHED'}

def register():
    bpy.utils.register_class(NyghtshadePanel)
    bpy.utils.register_class(AskAI)

def unregister():
    bpy.utils.unregister_class(NyghtshadePanel)

This gives a production grammar that NLP models can map to command intents.

import shutil

# Define the destination structure path
scaffold_root = "/mnt/data/nyghtshade_device_project"

# Define subdirectories
subdirs = [
    "cli",
    "desktop",
    "web",
    "plugins/unity",
    "plugins/unreal",
    "plugins/blender",
    "docs",
    "intents",
    "assets"
]

# Create folder structure
for subdir in subdirs:
    os.makedirs(os.path.join(scaffold_root, subdir), exist_ok=True)

# Move relevant files from extracted ZIPs into place
file_map = {
    # Plugins
    "braxtigconfig-ari/braxtigconfig-ari/Unity/FSM_Script.cs": "plugins/unity/FSM_Script.cs",
    "braxtigconfig-ari/braxtigconfig-ari/UE5/DialogueTreeComponent.txt": "plugins/unreal/DialogueTreeComponent.txt",
    "braxtigconfig-ari/braxtigconfig-ari/Blender/BridgetPathing.py": "plugins/blender/BridgetPathing.py",
    # Intent grammar placeholder
    "braxtigconfig-ari/braxtigconfig-ari/replit222.txt": "intents/intents.json",
    # CLI/Web starter files
    "braxtigconfig-ari/braxtigconfig-ari/index.js": "cli/index.js",
    # Assets
    "braxtigconfig-ari/braxtigconfig-ari/ChatGPT Image Dec 23, 2025, 12_12_15 AM.png": "assets/mockup.png"
}

# Copy the files
for src_rel, dest_rel in file_map.items():
    src = os.path.join("/mnt/data", src_rel)
    dest = os.path.join(scaffold_root, dest_rel)
    shutil.copy2(src, dest)

# Create placeholder files
with open(os.path.join(scaffold_root, "cli/main.py"), "w") as f:
    f.write("# Entry point for Nyghtshade CLI\nprint('Launching CLI...')\n")

with open(os.path.join(scaffold_root, "web/main.py"), "w") as f:
    f.write("# Placeholder for web entry\n")

with open(os.path.join(scaffold_root, "README.md"), "w") as f:
    f.write("# THE NYGHTSHADE DEVICE\n\nGame AI agent system for Unity, Unreal, and Blender with CLI and web interface.\n")

with open(os.path.join(scaffold_root, ".replit"), "w") as f:
    f.write("run = \"python3 cli/main.py\"\n")

with open(os.path.join(scaffold_root, "replit.nix"), "w") as f:
    f.write('''
{ pkgs }: {
  deps = [
    pkgs.python3
    pkgs.nodejs
  ];
}
''')

# Zip the final project
zip_output_path = "/mnt/data/nyghtshade-device-replit-ready.zip"
shutil.make_archive(zip_output_path.replace(".zip", ""), 'zip', scaffold_root)

Style Transfer / Face / Portrait Tools

Fotor AI – simple edits + styles

Picsart AI – social-friendly image generator

VIDEO GENERATORS

These make moving images from text or source clips.

Text-to-Video

Runway Gen-2 – one of the first actually usable text→video models

Pika Labs – clean, cinematic AI video generation

Kaiber – animate images / prompts

Synthesia – avatar video + voice generation

HeyGen – human avatars from text/script

Colossyan – AI presenter + language support

InVideo AI – quick social clips from text

Invideo + AI – template + AI generation

Pika AI – strong cinematic output

Video Editing / AI Assist

Runway (Gen-2 / Edit tools) – AI cut, replace, inpaint

Descript – auto transcribe + edit video by text

VEED.io – simpler social editor + AI tools

Adobe Premiere + Generative AI – patch edits

AUDIO / SPEECH (Related)

Not strictly video/image but often part of the ecosystem.

ElevenLabs – text-to-speech lifelike voices

Murf.ai – video narration + voices

Play.ht – voice generation

COMBOS & PLUG-INS (for UE5/Game Dev)

Runway + Unreal Bridge tools (experimental)

Kaedim3D – 2D→3D proxy generator (texture + mesh helpers)

NVIDIA Canvas / Picasso – paint to scene generation

Quick practical picks (so you don’t waste days)

If you want simple image generation → Midjourney / SDXL / Firefly
If you want animated video from prompts → Runway Gen-2 / Pika Labs
If you want avatar + dialog videos → Synthesia / HeyGen
If you want editor + AI assist → Descript / Runway editing suite

No magic wands: all of these still struggle with complex scenes, long story continuity, and high fidelity beyond a few seconds, but they exist and they work.

Key Concepts Explained:

Core Services take natural language + voice → interpret it → dispatch to the right tool.

Scene Analyzer reads a scene’s mesh graph and spits out actionable data (surface normals, bounds, slopes, etc.).

Asset Discovery crawls local and remote repos, labels assets, and catalogs them.

Plugin Bridge lets the assistant “live inside” external tools (Unity, Unreal, Blender, VS Code).

🌀 Blender Addon (Python)
bl_info = {
    "name": "Nyghtshade Assistant",
    "blender": (3, 0, 0),
    "category": "AI"
}

import bpy

class NyghtshadePanel(bpy.types.Panel):
    bl_label = "Nyghtshade"
    bl_idname = "NYGHTSHADE_PT_main"
    bl_space_type = 'VIEW_3D'

    def draw(self, context):
        layout = self.layout
        layout.operator("nyghtshade.ask_ai")

class AskAI(bpy.types.Operator):
    bl_idname = "nyghtshade.ask_ai"
    bl_label = "Ask AI"

    def execute(self, context):
        # send scene mesh + prompt
        return {'FINISHED'}

def register():
    bpy.utils.register_class(NyghtshadePanel)
    bpy.utils.register_class(AskAI)

def unregister():
    bpy.utils.unregister_class(NyghtshadePanel)

🗣️ Voice Command Grammar — Expanded (Intent Map)
Here’s a more structured grammar resembling SRGS (simplified):

<grammar version="1.0">
  <rule id="root">
    <one-of>
      <item> place <asset> (around | near | inside) <location> </item>
      <item> generate <script_type> for <purpose> </item>
      <item> find <asset_type> </item>
      <item> translate to <language> </item>
      <item> set theme to <theme> </item>
    </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="asset">
    <one-of> crate crates torch torches tree trees npc enemies </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="location">
    <one-of> castle keep forest path road </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="script_type">
    <one-of> C# Python blueprint behavior </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="language">
    <one-of> English Spanish Chinese French </one-of>
  </rule>

</grammar>
This gives a production grammar that NLP models can map to command intents.

🗣️ Voice Command Grammar — Expanded (Intent Map)
Here’s a more structured grammar resembling SRGS (simplified):
<grammar version="1.0"> <rule id="root"> <one-of> <item> place <asset> (around | near | inside) <location> </item> <item> generate <script_type> for <purpose> </item> <item> find <asset_type> </item> <item> translate to <language> </item> <item> set theme to <theme> </item> </one-of> </rule> <rule id="asset"> <one-of> crate crates torch torches tree trees npc enemies </one-of> </rule> <rule id="location"> <one-of> castle keep forest path road </one-of> </rule> <rule id="script_type"> <one-of> C# Python blueprint behavior </one-of> </rule> <rule id="language"> <one-of> English Spanish Chinese French </one-of> </rule> </grammar>
This gives a production grammar that NLP models can map to command intents.

# nyghtshade/main.py

import sys


def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this help menu
    """)


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder logic)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder layout logic)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code using AI... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not yet implemented")
    else:
        show_help()

🧪 cli/main.py
import sys

def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this help menu
    """)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder logic)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder layout logic)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code using AI... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not yet implemented")
    else:
        show_help()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

📌 cli/main.py
import sys

def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this menu
    """)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not implemented")
    else:
        show_help()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Skimmable (headers + bullets)

You said:
Jail commissaries: 'Mini convenience store' actually serves lofty goals
Beth Smithbethsmith@thegleaner.com
Oct. 25, 2016, 9:19 a.m. CT



A jail's commissary can be more than a place for inmates to purchase wanted items.

The "mini convenience store," as it's been described, can also be a tool for keeping inmates busy, and for maintaining order in facilities which often have large, potentially dangerous populations.

"When you have a large jail with a mixed population, you have to have vision or purpose which will benefit the inmates, as well as staff, and keep good behavior going," said Henderson County Jailer Ron Herrington.

The commissary, and the profits from it, are an important part of that, he said.

How it works, is "inmates who have deposited money, or if their family has deposited money into their fund, can use that money at the commissary to buy items they want," Herrington said. "We contract with Aramark for the commissary items because of their buying power. The jail receives a share of the profits from the commissary."

"The profits from the commissary account are used for inmates' well being," he explained, such as providing work and educational opportunities, funding rewards for good behavior and for when they reach certain goals in the Substance Abuse Program, and also as part of the Successful Transition Employment Education Program.

"Taxpayers do not pay for any of the rewards," Herrington said. "The incentive items or items for the well-being of the inmates are paid for from the jail canteen/commissary profits."

The money even helps to pay some inmate medical bills. "By law, we're allowed to pay certain medical bills with commissary profits," he said. "I have an inmate who is HIV positive. The medications for that inmate are extremely expensive and run around $10,000 a month. The commissary profits pay for that medicine," he said.

Get the Daily Briefing newsletter in your inbox.
Start your day with the morning's top news

Delivery: Daily
Your Email
The right to purchase items from the commissary is a privilege, explained HCDC Col. Leslie Gibson. "Those privileges can be restricted if there are behavioral problems," she said.

Other jails also use commissary profits to finance inmate-related needs and programs.

"We can use the profits we earn from the commissary accounts to maintain the lawn mowers" used by inmates to care for properties throughout the county, said Union County Jailer Shawn Elder. "These are tools which gets the inmates outside, give them work credit, and they are doing the community a favor." The Union County jail averages about 50 inmates daily, he said.


Webster County Jailer Terry Elder, who is no relation to Shawn Elder, also said canteen profits buy and maintain equipment such as lawnmowers and string trimmers used by inmates, who are able to work outside of the detention center. For those serving time, that's a tremendous privilege and reward. The Webster County jail has an average daily population of around 300 inmates.

HCDC Col. Leslie Gibson walks through the jail's commissary.
"We pay for their GED testing" also with canteen/commissary profits, as well as other educational programs, he said. "We try to do everything we can for the well-being of the inmates with the canteen profits because it's their money, not ours."

All three jailers said inmates at the respective facilities have access to television.

In Henderson County, Herrington said, "We buy televisions for each cell because by law, inmates must have access to the news, and we don't want to risk putting newspapers in the cells. We try to buy new televisions every three years. We donate the old televisions to nonprofit organizations or sell them to other counties for their jails," he said.

A painting submitted by an inmate for the Henderson County jail's art contest
Canteen profits pay for those televisions, as well as batteries for the remote controls, according to the local jail's canteen fund summary for 2015-16. And the money involved isn't trivial. As of June 30, 2016, the canteen/commissary fund for the Henderson County Detention Center showed a cash balance, after expenditures, of $463,598.


Vanderburgh County Sheriff David Wedding said canteen profits from the Vanderburgh County Detention Center are used "to fund fundamental needs at our jail such as our guards' clothing and their training."

"We also use some commissary funds on (inmate) programs such as substance abuse programs," he said.

While the Vanderburgh County Detention Center offers inmates addiction recovery and some educational opportunities, Wedding said, "Our jail is so crowded and somewhat short-staffed, so it's hard to initiate new programs when we are trying to adequately safeguard the inmates."

However, he said, "A big program we do have is called Recovery Works, an aftercare and follow-up after release from jail for mental health and addiction recovery."

While many might not see the need for inmates to be occupied with programs or have the opportunity to earn good behavior rewards, those working inside a correctional facility said the need is real.

"If you have 700 inmates and all they've got to do all day is to look at each other without work or learning activities," Herrington said, it can cause problems. "We don't want the jail torn up or inmates and correctional officers injured because of boredom."

Aramark Employee Terri Capps takes the jails commissary "Go Cart" to various cells, allowing inmates to purchase goods.
Occupying Union County inmates with outside work such as mowing and trimming public properties "helps keep the inmate population calm," added Jailer Shawn Elder.

Without something to do, he said, "They could flood their cells, tear up their cells, and they are already in jail so there aren't any repercussions ... Keeping them busy also cuts down on the fighting."

"The overall goal is we want their time consumed," Elder said. "We buy televisions, games, books ... you want to keep their minds busy."

"It's a fine line to walk because they are incarcerated," he said. "But you also need to treat inmates with respect."

Giving inmates the opportunity to work benefits not only them, but the county in which they are incarcerated, said Jailer Terry Elder.

"Inmate labor provides roughly $900,000 of in-kind services for the county," he said. "The work also keeps them calm. A lot of inmates have excellent skills. It makes you wonder why, with talent like that, they are in jail. But I guess they took a wrong turn somewhere."

On the flip side, while the inmate is working, he/she is shaving time off their sentence, he said. "We have inmates write us, asking us to let them come to our facility to serve their time, so they can work."

In the Vanderburgh County Detention Center. which averages 650 inmates daily, Sheriff Wedding said those incarcerated can earn the opportunity to work in the laundry room or kitchen detail. "These are coveted spots," he said. And "they have televisions and can have video visitations with their families. We don't cut them off from their families," he said.

Other ways to occupy an inmates time, he said, is through technology privileges. "They can rent a tablet on which they can watch movies, listen to music or text message their families," he said, adding that "we can monitor all correspondence."

"Most of our inmates are pretty compliant," Wedding said. "But some groups are always in trouble ... These are people who don't follow rules and that's why they are in custody."

"Jails can be a dangerous place," Herrington said. "But incentives and rewards are tools we use to encourage good behavior. We also want to keep providing programs to train inmates in work-related fields for when they leave incarceration."

The jail also organizes art contests, cooking contests, fishing contests, letter-writing contests and clean-cell contests. Prizes are paid for through the commissary profits.

"Inmates with the cleanest cells get their choice of dinner cooked from someplace other than the jail," Gibson said. "It does work to help keep the cells clean and clutter free."

For the cooking contests,Gibson said inmates can enter dishes they've developed using food items they purchase in the commissary and that can be assembled in their cells. Again prizes are paid for through the profits garnered from the commissary.

Sometimes, the only opportunity an inmate has to purchase anything through the commissary is after winning a prize in one of the contests, jail officials said.

One of the female inmates didn't have money for commissary goods or to purchase a phone card to call home, said HCDC Lt. Tabitha Vincent.

A painting by an inmate submitted to the Henderson Co. jail's art contest
"When she won the art contest, she bought a phone card for herself and for everyone in her cell," Vincent said.

"You have to remember that they are still people," Gibson said.

"I don't know what other jails do," Herrington said, "but these programs work for me at this facility."

1) Hit Contract Manager (UE5 C++)
// HitContract.h
USTRUCT(BlueprintType)
struct FHitContract {
  GENERATED_BODY()
  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) FString TargetId;
  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) bool bTargetIsPlayer;
  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) bool bAnonymousPlacer;
  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) int32 PayoutDC;
  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) bool bActive;
};

UCLASS(Blueprintable)
class UHitContractManager : public UObject {
  GENERATED_BODY()
public:
  UPROPERTY(BlueprintReadOnly) TArray<FHitContract> ActiveContracts;

  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
  void PlaceHit(const FHitContract& Contract);

  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
  bool AcceptHit(const FString& ContractId, const FString& PlayerId);

  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
  void ResolveHit(const FString& ContractId, bool bSuccess);
};
Notes

Validate Untouchables before PlaceHit.

On accept, mark contract “claimed” but not exclusive unless you want it to be.

2) PC Lockout System (Blueprint-Friendly)
// PlayerProtection.h
UCLASS(Blueprintable)
class UPlayerProtection : public UObject {
  GENERATED_BODY()
public:
  UPROPERTY(BlueprintReadOnly) TMap<FString, FDateTime> PCLockouts;

  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
  bool CanBeTargeted(const FString& PlayerId) const;

  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
  void ClaimPC(const FString& PlayerId);
};
Logic

ClaimPC sets Now + 48 hours.

CanBeTargeted checks lockout.

  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)

3️⃣ PC Lockout System (48 Real Hours)
UCLASS(Blueprintable)
class UPCService : public UObject {
  GENERATED_BODY()

  UPROPERTY()
  TMap<FString, FDateTime> PCLockouts;

public:
  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
  void ClaimPC(FString PlayerID) {
    PCLockouts.Add(PlayerID, FDateTime::UtcNow() + FTimespan::FromHours(48));
  }

  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
  bool IsTargetable(FString PlayerID) {
    if (!PCLockouts.Contains(PlayerID)) return true;
    return FDateTime::UtcNow() > PCLockouts[PlayerID];
  }
};

You said:
Jail commissaries: 'Mini convenience store' actually serves lofty goals
Beth Smithbethsmith@thegleaner.com
Oct. 25, 2016, 9:19 a.m. CT



A jail's commissary can be more than a place for inmates to purchase wanted items.

The "mini convenience store," as it's been described, can also be a tool for keeping inmates busy, and for maintaining order in facilities which often have large, potentially dangerous populations.

"When you have a large jail with a mixed population, you have to have vision or purpose which will benefit the inmates, as well as staff, and keep good behavior going," said Henderson County Jailer Ron Herrington.

The commissary, and the profits from it, are an important part of that, he said.

How it works, is "inmates who have deposited money, or if their family has deposited money into their fund, can use that money at the commissary to buy items they want," Herrington said. "We contract with Aramark for the commissary items because of their buying power. The jail receives a share of the profits from the commissary."

"The profits from the commissary account are used for inmates' well being," he explained, such as providing work and educational opportunities, funding rewards for good behavior and for when they reach certain goals in the Substance Abuse Program, and also as part of the Successful Transition Employment Education Program.

"Taxpayers do not pay for any of the rewards," Herrington said. "The incentive items or items for the well-being of the inmates are paid for from the jail canteen/commissary profits."

The money even helps to pay some inmate medical bills. "By law, we're allowed to pay certain medical bills with commissary profits," he said. "I have an inmate who is HIV positive. The medications for that inmate are extremely expensive and run around $10,000 a month. The commissary profits pay for that medicine," he said.

Get the Daily Briefing newsletter in your inbox.
Start your day with the morning's top news

Delivery: Daily
Your Email
The right to purchase items from the commissary is a privilege, explained HCDC Col. Leslie Gibson. "Those privileges can be restricted if there are behavioral problems," she said.

Other jails also use commissary profits to finance inmate-related needs and programs.

"We can use the profits we earn from the commissary accounts to maintain the lawn mowers" used by inmates to care for properties throughout the county, said Union County Jailer Shawn Elder. "These are tools which gets the inmates outside, give them work credit, and they are doing the community a favor." The Union County jail averages about 50 inmates daily, he said.


Webster County Jailer Terry Elder, who is no relation to Shawn Elder, also said canteen profits buy and maintain equipment such as lawnmowers and string trimmers used by inmates, who are able to work outside of the detention center. For those serving time, that's a tremendous privilege and reward. The Webster County jail has an average daily population of around 300 inmates.

HCDC Col. Leslie Gibson walks through the jail's commissary.
"We pay for their GED testing" also with canteen/commissary profits, as well as other educational programs, he said. "We try to do everything we can for the well-being of the inmates with the canteen profits because it's their money, not ours."

All three jailers said inmates at the respective facilities have access to television.

In Henderson County, Herrington said, "We buy televisions for each cell because by law, inmates must have access to the news, and we don't want to risk putting newspapers in the cells. We try to buy new televisions every three years. We donate the old televisions to nonprofit organizations or sell them to other counties for their jails," he said.

A painting submitted by an inmate for the Henderson County jail's art contest
Canteen profits pay for those televisions, as well as batteries for the remote controls, according to the local jail's canteen fund summary for 2015-16. And the money involved isn't trivial. As of June 30, 2016, the canteen/commissary fund for the Henderson County Detention Center showed a cash balance, after expenditures, of $463,598.


Vanderburgh County Sheriff David Wedding said canteen profits from the Vanderburgh County Detention Center are used "to fund fundamental needs at our jail such as our guards' clothing and their training."

"We also use some commissary funds on (inmate) programs such as substance abuse programs," he said.

While the Vanderburgh County Detention Center offers inmates addiction recovery and some educational opportunities, Wedding said, "Our jail is so crowded and somewhat short-staffed, so it's hard to initiate new programs when we are trying to adequately safeguard the inmates."

However, he said, "A big program we do have is called Recovery Works, an aftercare and follow-up after release from jail for mental health and addiction recovery."

While many might not see the need for inmates to be occupied with programs or have the opportunity to earn good behavior rewards, those working inside a correctional facility said the need is real.

"If you have 700 inmates and all they've got to do all day is to look at each other without work or learning activities," Herrington said, it can cause problems. "We don't want the jail torn up or inmates and correctional officers injured because of boredom."

Aramark Employee Terri Capps takes the jails commissary "Go Cart" to various cells, allowing inmates to purchase goods.
Occupying Union County inmates with outside work such as mowing and trimming public properties "helps keep the inmate population calm," added Jailer Shawn Elder.

Without something to do, he said, "They could flood their cells, tear up their cells, and they are already in jail so there aren't any repercussions ... Keeping them busy also cuts down on the fighting."

"The overall goal is we want their time consumed," Elder said. "We buy televisions, games, books ... you want to keep their minds busy."

"It's a fine line to walk because they are incarcerated," he said. "But you also need to treat inmates with respect."

Giving inmates the opportunity to work benefits not only them, but the county in which they are incarcerated, said Jailer Terry Elder.

"Inmate labor provides roughly $900,000 of in-kind services for the county," he said. "The work also keeps them calm. A lot of inmates have excellent skills. It makes you wonder why, with talent like that, they are in jail. But I guess they took a wrong turn somewhere."

On the flip side, while the inmate is working, he/she is shaving time off their sentence, he said. "We have inmates write us, asking us to let them come to our facility to serve their time, so they can work."

In the Vanderburgh County Detention Center. which averages 650 inmates daily, Sheriff Wedding said those incarcerated can earn the opportunity to work in the laundry room or kitchen detail. "These are coveted spots," he said. And "they have televisions and can have video visitations with their families. We don't cut them off from their families," he said.

Other ways to occupy an inmates time, he said, is through technology privileges. "They can rent a tablet on which they can watch movies, listen to music or text message their families," he said, adding that "we can monitor all correspondence."

"Most of our inmates are pretty compliant," Wedding said. "But some groups are always in trouble ... These are people who don't follow rules and that's why they are in custody."

"Jails can be a dangerous place," Herrington said. "But incentives and rewards are tools we use to encourage good behavior. We also want to keep providing programs to train inmates in work-related fields for when they leave incarceration."

The jail also organizes art contests, cooking contests, fishing contests, letter-writing contests and clean-cell contests. Prizes are paid for through the commissary profits.

"Inmates with the cleanest cells get their choice of dinner cooked from someplace other than the jail," Gibson said. "It does work to help keep the cells clean and clutter free."

For the cooking contests,Gibson said inmates can enter dishes they've developed using food items they purchase in the commissary and that can be assembled in their cells. Again prizes are paid for through the profits garnered from the commissary.

Sometimes, the only opportunity an inmate has to purchase anything through the commissary is after winning a prize in one of the contests, jail officials said.

One of the female inmates didn't have money for commissary goods or to purchase a phone card to call home, said HCDC Lt. Tabitha Vincent.

A painting by an inmate submitted to the Henderson Co. jail's art contest
"When she won the art contest, she bought a phone card for herself and for everyone in her cell," Vincent said.

"You have to remember that they are still people," Gibson said.

"I don't know what other jails do," Herrington said, "but these programs work for me at this facility."

3️⃣ PC Lockout System (48 Real Hours)
UCLASS(Blueprintable)
class UPCService : public UObject {
  GENERATED_BODY()

  UPROPERTY()
  TMap<FString, FDateTime> PCLockouts;

public:
  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
  void ClaimPC(FString PlayerID) {
    PCLockouts.Add(PlayerID, FDateTime::UtcNow() + FTimespan::FromHours(48));
  }

  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
  bool IsTargetable(FString PlayerID) {
    if (!PCLockouts.Contains(PlayerID)) return true;
    return FDateTime::UtcNow() > PCLockouts[PlayerID];
  }
};

🟣 3. UNITY C# PROCEDURAL GENERATOR (Prefab-Based)
Drop this script on an empty GameObject:
HousingUnitGenerator.cs

using UnityEngine;

public class HousingUnitGenerator : MonoBehaviour
{
    public GameObject rotundaPrefab;
    public GameObject cellPrefab;
    public GameObject roomPrefab;

    float floorHeight = 12f;

    void Start()
    {
        SpawnRotunda();
        SpawnWing(0);     // North
        SpawnWing(90);    // East
        SpawnWing(180);   // South
        SpawnWing(270);   // West
    }

    void SpawnRotunda()
    {
        Instantiate(rotundaPrefab, new Vector3(0,0,0), Quaternion.identity, transform);
    }

    void SpawnWing(float angle)
    {
        Quaternion rot = Quaternion.Euler(0, angle, 0);

        // Wing shell — center 150 ft out
        Vector3 mid = rot * new Vector3(0, 150, 0);

        Instantiate(roomPrefab, mid, rot, transform);

        // Generate cells
        for(int i = 0; i < 28; i++)
        {
            float y = 55 + (i * 10);

            Vector3 leftPos  = rot * new Vector3(-9, y, 0);
            Vector3 rightPos = rot * new Vector3(+9, y, 0);

            Instantiate(cellPrefab, leftPos,  rot, transform);
            Instantiate(cellPrefab, rightPos, rot, transform);
        }

        // Dayroom
        Instantiate(roomPrefab, rot * new Vector3(0,200,0), rot, transform);

        // Shower
        Instantiate(roomPrefab, rot * new Vector3(0,70,0), rot, transform);

        // Stairwell
        Instantiate(roomPrefab, rot * new Vector3(0,330,0), rot, transform);

        // Sally Port
        Instantiate(roomPrefab, rot * new Vector3(0,50,0), rot, transform);
    }
}
Unity eats this like breakfast.

🟣 4. BLENDER — PYTHON 3.6+ GENERATOR SCRIPT
Paste into Blender’s scripting panel.
This builds the entire unit in 3D with exact coordinates.

import bpy
from mathutils import Vector, Matrix
from math import radians

def spawn_cube(size, loc):
    bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cube_add(size=1, location=loc)
    obj = bpy.context.object
    obj.scale = (size[0]/2, size[1]/2, size[2]/2)
    return obj

def rot_point(x, y, angle):
    m = Matrix.Rotation(radians(angle), 4, 'Z')
    v = m @ Vector((x,y,0))
    return v.x, v.y

# ROTUNDA
bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cylinder_add(radius=45, depth=48, location=(0,0,24))

# CATWALK
bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cylinder_add(radius=55, depth=4, location=(0,0,12))

# WING FUNCTION
def spawn_wing(angle):
    # Wing shell
    x,y = rot_point(0,150,angle)
    spawn_cube((60,300,48),(x,y,24))

    # Cells
    for i in range(28):
        yoff = 55 + i*10
        lx,ly = rot_point(-9,yoff,angle)
        rx,ry = rot_point( 9,yoff,angle)

        spawn_cube((10,8,12),(lx,ly,6))
        spawn_cube((10,8,12),(rx,ry,6))

    # Dayroom
    x,y = rot_point(0,200,angle)
    spawn_cube((40,40,48),(x,y,24))

    # Shower
    x,y = rot_point(0,70,angle)
    spawn_cube((30,30,12),(x,y,6))

    # Stairwell
    x,y = rot_point(0,330,angle)
    spawn_cube((20,20,48),(x,y,24))

    # Sally Port
    x,y = rot_point(0,50,angle)
    spawn_cube((20,12,12),(x,y,6))

# Spawn all four wings
for ang in (0,90,180,270):
    spawn_wing(ang)
Run it → Blender spits out a full 3D Nightshade Hollow housing unit in under a second.

EVENT Construction
    CALL SpawnPerimeter()

FUNCTION SpawnPerimeter()
    // Outer wall: octagon with 8 segments
    FOR i = 0 → 7:
        Angle = i * 45
        Dist = (900/2)
        Loc = RotateVector((Dist,0,0), Angle)
        SpawnWallSegment(Length=330, Location=Loc, Rotation=Angle)

    // Triple fences
    Spacings = [20,15,25]
    Offset = 900/2 - 20
    FOR spacing in Spacings:
        Offset -= spacing
        FOR i = 0 → 7:
            Angle = i * 45
            Dist = Offset
            Loc = RotateVector((Dist,0,0),Angle)
            SpawnFenceSegment(Location=Loc, Rotation=Angle)

FUNCTION SpawnSpine()
    Y = 0
    FOR block in SpineBlocks:
        Size = block.Size
        Loc = (0, Y + Size.Y/2, 0)
        SpawnBox(Size, Loc)
        Y += Size.Y

FUNCTION SpawnHousing()
    // East side
    FOR i = 0 → 9:
        X = +600
        Y = i * 450
        SpawnHousingUnitAt((X,Y,0))

    // West side
    FOR i = 0 → 9:
        X = -600
        Y = i * 450
        SpawnHousingUnitAt((X,Y,0))

    SpawnBox(Size=Yard.Size, Location=Yard.CenterOffset)

🟣 3. UNITY — FULL COMPLEX GENERATOR (C#)
using UnityEngine;

public class PrisonGenerator : MonoBehaviour
{
    public GameObject wallPrefab;
    public GameObject fencePrefab;
    public GameObject spineBlockPrefab;
    public GameObject housingUnitPrefab;
    public GameObject yardPrefab;

    void Start()
    {
        SpawnPerimeter();
        SpawnSpine();
        SpawnHousing();
        SpawnYard();
    }

    void SpawnPerimeter()
    {
        float radius = 900f/2f;
        for(int i=0;i<8;i++)
        {
            float angle = i * 45f;
            Vector3 pos = Quaternion.Euler(0,angle,0) * new Vector3(radius,0,0);
            Instantiate(wallPrefab, pos, Quaternion.Euler(0,angle,0), transform);
        }
    }

    void SpawnSpine()
    {
        float yOffset = 0f;
        foreach(var b in SpineBlocks.Data)
        {
            Vector3 pos = new Vector3(0, 0, yOffset + b.size.y/2);
            Instantiate(spineBlockPrefab, pos, Quaternion.identity, transform);
            yOffset += b.size.y;
        }
    }

    void SpawnHousing()
    {
        for(int i=0;i<10;i++)
        {
            Instantiate(housingUnitPrefab, new Vector3(600,i*450,0), Quaternion.identity, transform);
            Instantiate(housingUnitPrefab, new Vector3(-600,i*450,0), Quaternion.identity, transform);
        }
    }

    void SpawnYard()
    {
        Instantiate(yardPrefab, new Vector3(-300,0,0), Quaternion.identity, transform);
    }
}

You said:
Jail commissaries: 'Mini convenience store' actually serves lofty goals
Beth Smithbethsmith@thegleaner.com
Oct. 25, 2016, 9:19 a.m. CT



A jail's commissary can be more than a place for inmates to purchase wanted items.

The "mini convenience store," as it's been described, can also be a tool for keeping inmates busy, and for maintaining order in facilities which often have large, potentially dangerous populations.

"When you have a large jail with a mixed population, you have to have vision or purpose which will benefit the inmates, as well as staff, and keep good behavior going," said Henderson County Jailer Ron Herrington.

The commissary, and the profits from it, are an important part of that, he said.

How it works, is "inmates who have deposited money, or if their family has deposited money into their fund, can use that money at the commissary to buy items they want," Herrington said. "We contract with Aramark for the commissary items because of their buying power. The jail receives a share of the profits from the commissary."

"The profits from the commissary account are used for inmates' well being," he explained, such as providing work and educational opportunities, funding rewards for good behavior and for when they reach certain goals in the Substance Abuse Program, and also as part of the Successful Transition Employment Education Program.

"Taxpayers do not pay for any of the rewards," Herrington said. "The incentive items or items for the well-being of the inmates are paid for from the jail canteen/commissary profits."

The money even helps to pay some inmate medical bills. "By law, we're allowed to pay certain medical bills with commissary profits," he said. "I have an inmate who is HIV positive. The medications for that inmate are extremely expensive and run around $10,000 a month. The commissary profits pay for that medicine," he said.

Get the Daily Briefing newsletter in your inbox.
Start your day with the morning's top news

Delivery: Daily
Your Email
The right to purchase items from the commissary is a privilege, explained HCDC Col. Leslie Gibson. "Those privileges can be restricted if there are behavioral problems," she said.

Other jails also use commissary profits to finance inmate-related needs and programs.

"We can use the profits we earn from the commissary accounts to maintain the lawn mowers" used by inmates to care for properties throughout the county, said Union County Jailer Shawn Elder. "These are tools which gets the inmates outside, give them work credit, and they are doing the community a favor." The Union County jail averages about 50 inmates daily, he said.


Webster County Jailer Terry Elder, who is no relation to Shawn Elder, also said canteen profits buy and maintain equipment such as lawnmowers and string trimmers used by inmates, who are able to work outside of the detention center. For those serving time, that's a tremendous privilege and reward. The Webster County jail has an average daily population of around 300 inmates.

HCDC Col. Leslie Gibson walks through the jail's commissary.
"We pay for their GED testing" also with canteen/commissary profits, as well as other educational programs, he said. "We try to do everything we can for the well-being of the inmates with the canteen profits because it's their money, not ours."

All three jailers said inmates at the respective facilities have access to television.

In Henderson County, Herrington said, "We buy televisions for each cell because by law, inmates must have access to the news, and we don't want to risk putting newspapers in the cells. We try to buy new televisions every three years. We donate the old televisions to nonprofit organizations or sell them to other counties for their jails," he said.

A painting submitted by an inmate for the Henderson County jail's art contest
Canteen profits pay for those televisions, as well as batteries for the remote controls, according to the local jail's canteen fund summary for 2015-16. And the money involved isn't trivial. As of June 30, 2016, the canteen/commissary fund for the Henderson County Detention Center showed a cash balance, after expenditures, of $463,598.


Vanderburgh County Sheriff David Wedding said canteen profits from the Vanderburgh County Detention Center are used "to fund fundamental needs at our jail such as our guards' clothing and their training."

"We also use some commissary funds on (inmate) programs such as substance abuse programs," he said.

While the Vanderburgh County Detention Center offers inmates addiction recovery and some educational opportunities, Wedding said, "Our jail is so crowded and somewhat short-staffed, so it's hard to initiate new programs when we are trying to adequately safeguard the inmates."

However, he said, "A big program we do have is called Recovery Works, an aftercare and follow-up after release from jail for mental health and addiction recovery."

While many might not see the need for inmates to be occupied with programs or have the opportunity to earn good behavior rewards, those working inside a correctional facility said the need is real.

"If you have 700 inmates and all they've got to do all day is to look at each other without work or learning activities," Herrington said, it can cause problems. "We don't want the jail torn up or inmates and correctional officers injured because of boredom."

Aramark Employee Terri Capps takes the jails commissary "Go Cart" to various cells, allowing inmates to purchase goods.
Occupying Union County inmates with outside work such as mowing and trimming public properties "helps keep the inmate population calm," added Jailer Shawn Elder.

Without something to do, he said, "They could flood their cells, tear up their cells, and they are already in jail so there aren't any repercussions ... Keeping them busy also cuts down on the fighting."

"The overall goal is we want their time consumed," Elder said. "We buy televisions, games, books ... you want to keep their minds busy."

"It's a fine line to walk because they are incarcerated," he said. "But you also need to treat inmates with respect."

Giving inmates the opportunity to work benefits not only them, but the county in which they are incarcerated, said Jailer Terry Elder.

"Inmate labor provides roughly $900,000 of in-kind services for the county," he said. "The work also keeps them calm. A lot of inmates have excellent skills. It makes you wonder why, with talent like that, they are in jail. But I guess they took a wrong turn somewhere."

On the flip side, while the inmate is working, he/she is shaving time off their sentence, he said. "We have inmates write us, asking us to let them come to our facility to serve their time, so they can work."

In the Vanderburgh County Detention Center. which averages 650 inmates daily, Sheriff Wedding said those incarcerated can earn the opportunity to work in the laundry room or kitchen detail. "These are coveted spots," he said. And "they have televisions and can have video visitations with their families. We don't cut them off from their families," he said.

Other ways to occupy an inmates time, he said, is through technology privileges. "They can rent a tablet on which they can watch movies, listen to music or text message their families," he said, adding that "we can monitor all correspondence."

"Most of our inmates are pretty compliant," Wedding said. "But some groups are always in trouble ... These are people who don't follow rules and that's why they are in custody."

"Jails can be a dangerous place," Herrington said. "But incentives and rewards are tools we use to encourage good behavior. We also want to keep providing programs to train inmates in work-related fields for when they leave incarceration."

The jail also organizes art contests, cooking contests, fishing contests, letter-writing contests and clean-cell contests. Prizes are paid for through the commissary profits.

"Inmates with the cleanest cells get their choice of dinner cooked from someplace other than the jail," Gibson said. "It does work to help keep the cells clean and clutter free."

For the cooking contests,Gibson said inmates can enter dishes they've developed using food items they purchase in the commissary and that can be assembled in their cells. Again prizes are paid for through the profits garnered from the commissary.

Sometimes, the only opportunity an inmate has to purchase anything through the commissary is after winning a prize in one of the contests, jail officials said.

One of the female inmates didn't have money for commissary goods or to purchase a phone card to call home, said HCDC Lt. Tabitha Vincent.

A painting by an inmate submitted to the Henderson Co. jail's art contest
"When she won the art contest, she bought a phone card for herself and for everyone in her cell," Vincent said.

"You have to remember that they are still people," Gibson said.

"I don't know what other jails do," Herrington said, "but these programs work for me at this facility."

⭐ 2. TATTOO SYSTEM — UNITY
public IEnumerator ApplyTattoo(Player target, TattooData data)
{
    float time = 300f; // 5 minutes
    while (time > 0)
    {
        time -= Time.deltaTime;
        UI_TattooProgress.Update(time);
        yield return null;
    }

    target.TattooManager.AddTattoo(data);
}
Tattoo remains even on failure.

    if (Random.value > chance) return false;

    this.isBribed = true;
    return true;
}

🟣 3. UNITY C# PROCEDURAL GENERATOR (Prefab-Based)

HousingUnitGenerator.cs

using UnityEngine;

public class HousingUnitGenerator : MonoBehaviour
{
    public GameObject rotundaPrefab;
    public GameObject cellPrefab;
    public GameObject roomPrefab;

    float floorHeight = 12f;

    void Start()
    {
        SpawnRotunda();
        SpawnWing(0);     // North
        SpawnWing(90);    // East
        SpawnWing(180);   // South
        SpawnWing(270);   // West
    }

    void SpawnRotunda()
    {
        Instantiate(rotundaPrefab, new Vector3(0,0,0), Quaternion.identity, transform);
    }

    void SpawnWing(float angle)
    {
        Quaternion rot = Quaternion.Euler(0, angle, 0);

        // Wing shell — center 150 ft out
        Vector3 mid = rot * new Vector3(0, 150, 0);

        Instantiate(roomPrefab, mid, rot, transform);

        // Generate cells
        for(int i = 0; i < 28; i++)
        {
            float y = 55 + (i * 10);

            Vector3 leftPos  = rot * new Vector3(-9, y, 0);
            Vector3 rightPos = rot * new Vector3(+9, y, 0);

            Instantiate(cellPrefab, leftPos,  rot, transform);
            Instantiate(cellPrefab, rightPos, rot, transform);
        }

        // Dayroom
        Instantiate(roomPrefab, rot * new Vector3(0,200,0), rot, transform);

        // Shower
        Instantiate(roomPrefab, rot * new Vector3(0,70,0), rot, transform);

        // Stairwell
        Instantiate(roomPrefab, rot * new Vector3(0,330,0), rot, transform);

        // Sally Port
        Instantiate(roomPrefab, rot * new Vector3(0,50,0), rot, transform);
    }
}

🟣 4. BLENDER — PYTHON 3.6+ GENERATOR SCRIPT
Paste into Blender’s scripting panel.
This builds the entire unit in 3D with exact coordinates.

import bpy
from mathutils import Vector, Matrix
from math import radians

def spawn_cube(size, loc):
    bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cube_add(size=1, location=loc)
    obj = bpy.context.object
    obj.scale = (size[0]/2, size[1]/2, size[2]/2)
    return obj

def rot_point(x, y, angle):
    m = Matrix.Rotation(radians(angle), 4, 'Z')
    v = m @ Vector((x,y,0))
    return v.x, v.y

# ROTUNDA
bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cylinder_add(radius=45, depth=48, location=(0,0,24))

# CATWALK
bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cylinder_add(radius=55, depth=4, location=(0,0,12))

# WING FUNCTION
def spawn_wing(angle):
    # Wing shell
    x,y = rot_point(0,150,angle)
    spawn_cube((60,300,48),(x,y,24))

    # Cells
    for i in range(28):
        yoff = 55 + i*10
        lx,ly = rot_point(-9,yoff,angle)
        rx,ry = rot_point( 9,yoff,angle)

        spawn_cube((10,8,12),(lx,ly,6))
        spawn_cube((10,8,12),(rx,ry,6))

    # Dayroom
    x,y = rot_point(0,200,angle)
    spawn_cube((40,40,48),(x,y,24))

    # Shower
    x,y = rot_point(0,70,angle)
    spawn_cube((30,30,12),(x,y,6))

    # Stairwell
    x,y = rot_point(0,330,angle)
    spawn_cube((20,20,48),(x,y,24))

    # Sally Port
    x,y = rot_point(0,50,angle)
    spawn_cube((20,12,12),(x,y,6))

# Spawn all four wings
for ang in (0,90,180,270):
    spawn_wing(ang)
Run it → Blender spits out a full 3D Nightshade Hollow housing unit in under a second.

FUNCTION SpawnPerimeter()
    // Outer wall: octagon with 8 segments
    FOR i = 0 → 7:
        Angle = i * 45
        Dist = (900/2)
        Loc = RotateVector((Dist,0,0), Angle)
        SpawnWallSegment(Length=330, Location=Loc, Rotation=Angle)

    // Triple fences
    Spacings = [20,15,25]
    Offset = 900/2 - 20
    FOR spacing in Spacings:
        Offset -= spacing
        FOR i = 0 → 7:
            Angle = i * 45
            Dist = Offset
            Loc = RotateVector((Dist,0,0),Angle)
            SpawnFenceSegment(Location=Loc, Rotation=Angle)

FUNCTION SpawnSpine()
    Y = 0
    FOR block in SpineBlocks:
        Size = block.Size
        Loc = (0, Y + Size.Y/2, 0)
        SpawnBox(Size, Loc)
        Y += Size.Y

FUNCTION SpawnHousing()
    // East side
    FOR i = 0 → 9:
        X = +600
        Y = i * 450
        SpawnHousingUnitAt((X,Y,0))

    // West side
    FOR i = 0 → 9:
        X = -600
        Y = i * 450
        SpawnHousingUnitAt((X,Y,0))

    SpawnBox(Size=Yard.Size, Location=Yard.CenterOffset)

🟣 3. UNITY — FULL COMPLEX GENERATOR (C#)
using UnityEngine;

public class PrisonGenerator : MonoBehaviour
{
    public GameObject wallPrefab;
    public GameObject fencePrefab;
    public GameObject spineBlockPrefab;
    public GameObject housingUnitPrefab;
    public GameObject yardPrefab;

    void Start()
    {
        SpawnPerimeter();
        SpawnSpine();
        SpawnHousing();
        SpawnYard();
    }

    void SpawnPerimeter()
    {
        float radius = 900f/2f;
        for(int i=0;i<8;i++)
        {
            float angle = i * 45f;
            Vector3 pos = Quaternion.Euler(0,angle,0) * new Vector3(radius,0,0);
            Instantiate(wallPrefab, pos, Quaternion.Euler(0,angle,0), transform);
        }
    }

    void SpawnSpine()
    {
        float yOffset = 0f;
        foreach(var b in SpineBlocks.Data)
        {
            Vector3 pos = new Vector3(0, 0, yOffset + b.size.y/2);
            Instantiate(spineBlockPrefab, pos, Quaternion.identity, transform);
            yOffset += b.size.y;
        }
    }

    void SpawnHousing()
    {
        for(int i=0;i<10;i++)
        {
            Instantiate(housingUnitPrefab, new Vector3(600,i*450,0), Quaternion.identity, transform);
            Instantiate(housingUnitPrefab, new Vector3(-600,i*450,0), Quaternion.identity, transform);
        }
    }

    void SpawnYard()
    {
        Instantiate(yardPrefab, new Vector3(-300,0,0), Quaternion.identity, transform);
    }
}

from PIL import Image
from fpdf import FPDF
import os

# File paths (uploaded files)
file_paths = [
    "/mnt/data/spm1.jpg",
    "/mnt/data/spm2.jpg",
    "/mnt/data/spm3.webp",
    "/mnt/data/spm4.webp",
    "/mnt/data/spm5.webp"
]

# Convert webp images to RGB JPEGs for consistency and compatibility with FPDF
converted_images = []
for i, path in enumerate(file_paths):
    img = Image.open(path).convert("RGB")
    temp_path = f"/mnt/data/converted_spm_{i+1}.jpg"
    img.save(temp_path, "JPEG")
    converted_images.append(temp_path)

# Create a PDF document with 8.5x11 inch page (US Letter)
pdf = FPDF(unit="in", format="Letter")
pdf.add_page()

# Set margins
margin = 0.25
usable_width = 8.5 - 2 * margin
usable_height = 11 - 2 * margin

# Calculate image size for layout (5 images)
img_width = usable_width / 2
img_height = usable_height / 3

# Layout images in 2 columns, 3 rows (last row with one image centered)
positions = [
    (margin, margin),
    (margin + img_width, margin),
    (margin, margin + img_height),
    (margin + img_width, margin + img_height),
    ((8.5 - img_width) / 2, margin + 2 * img_height)  # Centered last image
]

for img_path, (x, y) in zip(converted_images, positions):
    pdf.image(img_path, x=x, y=y, w=img_width, h=img_height)

# Save PDF
output_pdf_path = "/mnt/data/SpiderMan_Printable_Collage.pdf"
pdf.output(output_pdf_path)

output_pdf_path

Fantastic. We’re digging into Windows licensing at midnight like it’s a spy movie. Living the dream.

Here’s the clean, no-nonsense way to pull your Windows product key using CMD.

METHOD 1: CMD (Run as Admin)
This works only if your key is embedded in BIOS/UEFI. Most OEM laptops are. Custom builds usually laugh at this.

Hit Start

Type cmd

Right-click Command Prompt

Choose Run as administrator

Paste this sacred incantation:

wmic path softwarelicensingservice get OA3xOriginalProductKey
Press Enter

If you see a 25-character key:
Congrats. That’s your Windows key. Guard it like it owes you money.

If it’s blank:
That means one of the following:

Windows was activated via digital license

You upgraded from an older version

Microsoft decided you don’t need to know anymore

Which, honestly, tracks.

METHOD 2: PowerShell (More reliable, still annoying)
Right-click Start

Select Windows PowerShell (Admin)

Paste this:

(Get-WmiObject -query 'select * from SoftwareLicensingService').OA3xOriginalProductKey
Same rules apply. If it shows up, great. If not, Microsoft is holding it hostage in the cloud.

IMPORTANT REALITY CHECK
If your Windows says “Activated with a digital license”, there is no full key stored locally. That’s normal. You don’t actually need the key to reinstall on the same machine.

To check activation status:

slmgr /xpr
Or go to:
Settings → System → Activation

TL;DR (For Humans With Better Things To Do)
OEM laptop? CMD method usually works.

Custom PC or upgraded Windows? No key stored.

Digital license? Reinstall and sign in. Microsoft remembers. Creepy but useful.

If you’re trying to reinstall, transfer, or nuke the OS and start fresh, I’ll tell you the exact move that won’t screw you later. I complain, but I don’t let people brick their machines.

ChatGPT said:
Fine. You want PowerShell. The grown-up tool. Respect.

Here’s a clean, copy-paste PowerShell script that does everything at once:
tries to pull the embedded key, checks activation type, and tells you what reality you’re stuck in.

Run PowerShell as Administrator first. Yes, actually do that.

PowerShell Script: Windows Key + Activation Status
Write-Host "=== Windows License Check ===" -ForegroundColor Cyan

# Try to get OEM key from BIOS/UEFI
$Key = (Get-WmiObject -Query "SELECT * FROM SoftwareLicensingService").OA3xOriginalProductKey

if ($Key) {
    Write-Host "OEM Product Key Found:" -ForegroundColor Green
    Write-Host $Key -ForegroundColor Yellow
} else {
    Write-Host "No OEM product key found in BIOS/UEFI." -ForegroundColor Red
    Write-Host "Likely activated via Digital License." -ForegroundColor DarkYellow
}

# Activation status
$License = Get-CimInstance SoftwareLicensingProduct |
Where-Object { $_.PartialProductKey -and $_.ApplicationID -match "55c92734-d682-4d71-983e-d6ec3f16059f" }

if ($License) {
    Write-Host "`nActivation Status:" -ForegroundColor Cyan
    Write-Host "License Status: $($License.LicenseStatus)" -ForegroundColor Yellow
    Write-Host "Partial Product Key: $($License.PartialProductKey)" -ForegroundColor Yellow
} else {
    Write-Host "`nNo active Windows license object found." -ForegroundColor Red
}

Write-Host "`nDone." -ForegroundColor Cyan
How to Run It (because someone always skips this)
Right-click Start

Click Windows PowerShell (Admin)

Paste the script

Press Enter

Stare at the truth Microsoft reveals to you

How to Read the Results (important part)
OEM Product Key Found

That’s your full 25-character key.

Save it somewhere safe. Not a sticky note. Not a screenshot. Not your brain.

No OEM key

You’re on a digital license

Reinstall Windows on the same machine → sign in → it auto-activates

No key required, no ritual sacrifice needed

Partial Product Key

This is normal

Windows only exposes the last 5 characters for verification

Blunt Bottom Line
Laptop / prebuilt: script usually works

Custom PC / upgraded Windows: digital license only

ChatGPT said:
Short answer first, because suspense is overrated:

No. You cannot legally use that key on a new PC.

Long answer, with the fine print Microsoft hopes you won’t read.

What actually happens if you move the SSD
You can physically take the SSD out and put it in a new PC. Silicon doesn’t care about licensing.

Windows will boot or at least try to.

Windows will then look around, see a different motherboard, and go:

“I don’t know this place.”

Result: Windows deactivates. Sometimes immediately. Sometimes after a reboot. Sometimes after it pretends everything is fine and then pulls the rug out.

Why the key won’t transfer
That key you pulled is an OEM key.

OEM keys are:

Locked to the original motherboard

Meant for one machine, forever

Not portable, not transferable, not sentimental

Moving the SSD does not move the license. The license lives with the motherboard like a cursed heirloom.

What you can do on the new PC
You have three sane options:

Option 1: Buy a new Windows license
Retail key, not OEM

Costs money, yes

Transfers to future PCs, unlike OEM garbage

Option 2: Install Windows without a key
Windows will run unactivated

You lose personalization and get a watermark

Functionally usable, aesthetically depressing

Option 3: If you had a retail key originally
You could transfer it

You don’t. This one is OEM. End of story.

Important clarification (because people get this wrong)
If you:

Replace the motherboard = license dies

Replace GPU, RAM, SSD = license survives

Move SSD to new PC = license does not follow

Microsoft doesn’t care about your feelings. It cares about motherboard serials.

Practical recommendation
If you’re building a new PC:

Install Windows clean

Either buy a retail key or live with unactivated until you do

Keep this OEM key tied to the old machine forever

If you want, I can:

Tell you exactly which Windows license type to buy so you never deal with this again

Or give you the cleanest way to reuse that SSD without dragging activation junk along with it

No follow-up question needed. You already know what you’re doing.

That’s it. Text in. Video out.

3. The controls you actually use
When available, you’ll see options like:

Video length (short clips, not feature films)

Aspect ratio (16:9, vertical, etc.)

Style (realistic, animated, cinematic, surreal)

No timeline. No keyframes. You steer with language like a civilized person.

4. How to get good results (this is the part people skip)
Use this order every time:

Camera – angle, movement, distance

Environment – location, time of day, weather

Subjects – people, buildings, objects

Action – what is happening over time

Style – realistic, cinematic, grain, color

Quality tags – filmic, detailed, high fidelity

Example:

Slow tracking shot through a prison rotunda, four cellblock wings branching outward, guards walking patrols below, inmates visible behind bars on upper tiers, sodium lights casting harsh shadows, gritty realistic style, cinematic depth of field

5. Iteration (aka how pros use it)
You do not get it perfect on the first try. Anyone who says otherwise is lying or lucky.

You:

Generate

Say “same shot but closer camera”

Or “remove people”

Or “nighttime with rain”

Or “more brutalist architecture”

Sora remembers context per run and refines instead of starting from scratch.

6. How it fits your prison game (important)
Use Sora to:

Visualize Nyghtshade Hollow exterior shots

Test mood, scale, lighting, and atmosphere

Create cinematic references for UE5 builds

Generate trailer-style footage concepts

Then you rebuild it properly in Unreal with real geometry, collision, AI, and gameplay. Sora is the sketch. UE5 is the steel and concrete.

7. Reality check
You cannot export meshes.

You cannot export levels.

You cannot press a button and get a game.

It gives you moving concept art, not miracles.

That’s the system. Simple, powerful, slightly unfair to artists who had to do this by hand for decades. Use it like a tool, not a wish-granting genie, and it behaves.

And no, you don’t “unlock” it by asking nicely. If it’s available, it shows up. If not, patience. Everyone hates that part.

Audio: Low ambient hum of the prison’s HVAC, distant clanks.
Visual: Plaque on the wall reads Ravencliff Lockdown Penitentiary. Ghost (X) sits at the far end of the table like the room’s anchor — relaxed, coiled. Staff and two lieutenants sit at mid-table, tense.

Shot 2 — Door / Entrance
Camera: Rack focus to the double doors as they open. Low-angle shot capturing Valley’s silhouette framed by light from the hallway.
Visual: Valley enters, suit impeccable, shoulders back. The room inhales. He stops at the opposite end of the table and plants himself opposite Ghost — deliberate, measured. He does not sit.

Micro-behaviors:

Valley’s suit whispers as he moves; cuffs immaculate.

Ghost watches him without flinching; eyes narrowed in appraisal.

A junior officer fumbles a folder; everyone stares.

Dialogue — Opening Exchange (Quiet, knife-sharp)
Junior Officer (stammering): “Warden Calla—”
Valley (soft, casual): “Valley is fine.” (he lets it land; no correction)

Camera: Close-up on Ghost — small eyebrow lift. He registers the name like a small, relevant file.

Ghost (cool): “You look expensive.” (half-smile; equal parts observation and test)
Valley (tilt of head, amused): “I prefer to be well-invested.” (brief pause — then) “We need to talk yard discipline and the new containment rotations.” (business, then personal)

Shot 3 — The Tension Slide
Camera: Over-the-shoulder pair — Ghost to Valley, then Valley to Ghost. Slow push to capture breathing cadence; both men framed like bookends.
Visual cues:

Valley rests one hand lightly on the table; knuckles hidden.

Ghost’s fingers drum the wood once, twice — a yard rhythm.

Ghost (low): “You ran the brief I sent?”
Valley: “I read it. I also read the yard.” (a beat) “It runs because of you, X. I don’t want to change that. I want to understand it.”

(This line flips the expected power dynamic — respect before control.)

Shot 4 — The Tease / Challenge
Camera: Medium, chest-up on Valley; subtle dolly in to feel the tease.
Valley (mild smile): “I hear you’re the undefeated champion on the yard. If you ever want a sparring partner — inform me. I’m not just a shiny suit.”
Ghost (calm, almost amused): “You looking for competition, or just a lesson in humility?”
Valley (soft): “Maybe both.” (no bravado; a promise)

Micro-reaction: Ghost’s jaw tightens a hair; an unreadable grin flickers. He does not correct Valley’s use of “X.” That matters.

Cut — Corridor → Yard Approach
Transition: Valley leaves the room; camera tracks him down the polished corridor. Cut to exterior yard gate swinging open. The sun slants low — the yard is a field of long shadows and diesel-gray gravel.

Shot 5 — Valley Enters the Yard
Camera: Wide establishing shot, then quick cuts to inmates — phones, murmurs, hardened faces turning.
Visual: Valley strides to the yard perimeter; inmates quiet, instinctively forming a respectful circle. The octagon sits center-stage.

Inmate Reactions:

Whisper: “That’s the new warden.”

Old-timer: “He walks like he owns a skyline.”

Teen faction member, impressed: “Yo—he’s built.”

Loyal Ghost followers exchange a look: curiosity laced with protectiveness.

Shot 6 — Face-Off Bench
Camera: Ground-level, slow pan from Ghost seated on his bench to Valley pausing at the octagon gate. The two are now physically in the same space; the yard’s energy hums louder.

Action: Valley lifts a hand in a formal but casual nod to the octagon; Ghost stands, muscles unworried, unshaken. The distance between them becomes a charged line.

Valley (loud enough for circle): “If you ever want a sparring session — properly, rules and med staff in place — I’ll take the opposite corner.”
Ghost (only to Valley, almost a whisper but audible): “Bring rules. Bring a good jaw.” (half grin)

Shot 7 — Crowd Close-Ups
Camera: Montage of faces — factions, ladies in the infirmary window, Bridget watching from the infirmary balcony with a notebook half-open. Her expression is an unreadable mix of concern and fascination.
Audio: Low murmurs swell into a beat: this is now a yard event.

Shot 8 — Closing Beat / Foreshadow
Camera: High crane shot pulling up and away; octagon centered like a stage. The two men remain, one seated and calm, one standing and composed. The yard circles like planets.
Voice-over (Ghost, internal, very low): “Nothing ever shakes me.”
Cut to black.

Notes for Performance, Blocking & Direction
Lighting: Conference room — warm, low-key, authoritative. Yard — late-afternoon, high contrast, emphasizing muscle and silhouette. Keep Valley’s wardrobe glossier; Ghost’s textures more worn.

Sound Design: Shoes against wood; fabric whispers; distant metallic clangs; ambient yard chatter that tightens into a hush when Valley enters.

Bridget’s role in this scene: Observer, the quiet emotional register. She notices micro-expressions — the almost-smile, the tightened breath — and will later be the one to translate physical tension into emotional explanation for both.

Camera language: Use longer holds on micro-expressions; save quick cuts for crowd reaction and the approach to octagon. Low-angle shots on Valley emphasize authority and size; medium, level shots on Ghost emphasize unshakable centeredness.

Acting direction: Both men are alpha; neither wins the room by force. It’s mutual sizing, curiosity, and buried history. Valley’s charm is controlled. Ghost’s calm is elemental.

Bridget becomes the emotional pivot — tending to both men as events escalate.
